item.title: The 6 Principles of Sexual Health
item.description:
Sex

The 6 Principles of Sexual Health

Key questions to ask yourself and your sexual partners.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Healthy sex lives require partners to align on sexual values and reach joint agreements.
  • Avoiding sexual conversations leads to issues that can erode intimacy and relationship trust.
  • True sexual health centers on ongoing consent from all partners.

This post is Part 1 of a series.

When people come in for sex therapy, they’ll often ask their sex therapist questions like, “How often should I (or we in the case of a couple) be having sex?” or “Is it normal for me (or for my partner) to desire to do ‘xyz type’ of sex?” or “Does it mean I’m an awful person if I fantasize about an ex-partner when I’m with my current spouse?”

Source: Mikhail Nilov/Pexels

Douglas Braun-Harvey and Michael Vigorito, authors of Treating Out of Control Sexual Behavior: Rethinking Sex Addiction, created a template for therapists to use when helping clients assess through self-inquiry whether their sex life is in fact sexually healthy. They called this assessment the Six Principles of Sexual Health. They created this model after years of treating mostly male-identified clients who were coming to therapy due to sexual behavior that was described as compulsive, hypersexual, or out-of-control. However, this framework could be adapted for any person who wants to optimize their sexual and relational wellness to better reflect their authentic values and priorities. A healthy sex life isn’t solely based on things like frequency or STI and pregnancy protection. Instead, it’s built on key principles that support an honest inquiry into the physical, emotional, psychological, ethical, and relationship behaviors and considerations one makes to live an authentic and integrated life as it relates to sexuality.

Consent: Each Partner Feels Free to Say No

Source: Tiger Lily/Pexels

This is perhaps the most important and basic principle of sexual health. Consent must be ongoing, not a one-off question that one asks at the initiation of a sexual encounter, whether with a new partner or a longstanding partner. Each person must feel emotionally safe and confident enough to pause or stop a behavior whenever they choose, even if they are in the middle of the experience to which they had initially agreed. If one partner agrees to go along with sex in order to avoid a conflict or because their partner will act in a resentful fashion if they say no, this isn't healthy sexuality, and it is not considered fully consensual. So while verbally agreeing to a specific sexual encounter is legal consent, if either partner feels pressure to keep going despite feeling afraid, anxious, or disassociated, the sex is no longer fully emotionally consensual. Depending on the relationship power dynamic, it could also be construed as coercive.

This kind of "going along" is reported frequently by female clients who present in sex therapy within their heterosexual experiences because they feel like they should, or ought to do it. However, many men also push through doubts or ambivalence in heterosexual or same gender sex because they are avoiding appearing less "like a real man." These are ingrained beliefs that are part of the heteronormative, patriarchal system, and oftentimes lead men to develop erectile disorder or premature ejaculation. These "going along" sexual encounters are not what is considered enthusiastic ongoing consent, and if repeated for months or even years, can lead to people losing connection or going underground with their own authentic desire and needs. Sex therapy with a certified sex therapist can re-educate and support clients to lead a more authentic sex life in which either partner feels free to say "no, not tonight" without feeling guilt, remorse, or shame.

Honesty: Being Able to Talk About Sex

A healthy sex life depends on both partners feeling comfortable communicating openly about their sexual relationship, including their desires, boundaries, concerns, and changing needs. A couple with a healthy sex life would be able to speak about topics such as fantasies, desire, boundaries, frequency, and any sexual discomfort. Honest conversation means addressing concerns before they turn into longstanding issues. Avoiding these conversations often negatively impacts the erotic foundations of a romantic relationship. A healthy couple is able to have a clear conversation that avoids blaming or shaming of or by either partner. For example, one partner might say, "I've noticed my desire has been lower lately. I don't think it's about you, but I'd like us to figure it out together." Open conversations like this strengthen intimacy.

Shared Values: Being on the Same Team

Though you don’t necessarily need to have the same beliefs to have successful relationships, it’s important that you have shared values when it comes to erotic and sexual agreements. Compatibility goes beyond libido and can extend into beliefs on topics such as monogamy, pornography, flirting, kinks, and so on. Partners need to be able to discuss what sex means to each of them in the relationship. A couple should be able to explore differing views on topics and come to a reasonable agreement that leaves both partners feeling safe and excited. For example, if one person in the couple enjoys watching porn and the other doesn’t, a healthy couple should be able to discuss the reasons for one’s interest and use of pornography and why the other feels discomfort around the behavior. Partners need to come to a joint agreement with one another on all sexual and erotic practices, whether they are done in private or with one another.

item.title: Courageous Optimism Does Not Always Wear a Badge
item.description:
Positive Psychology

Courageous Optimism Does Not Always Wear a Badge

Ordinary people are capable of extraordinary heroics, but preparation is key.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Courageous Optimism—the union of moral will, moral skill, and courage—isn't limited to law enforcement.
  • Recent civilian rescues highlight ordinary courage built through deliberate and extraordinary preparation.
  • Self-efficacy and self-determination are trainable, not just traits reserved for the courage behind the badge.

A few years ago, I set out to answer a narrow, almost tactical question asked of me by the incomparable Dr. Marty Seligman: What makes a police officer run toward gunfire when every instinct in the human body, and every civilian standing nearby, is oriented toward running away? The psychological theory I built to answer that question, Courageous Optimism, rests on three components: moral will, the desire to act rightly; moral skill, the trained competence to act effectively; and courage, the capacity to carry both past fear. I have applied that framework almost exclusively to law enforcement, because as a retired police officer, that is the world I know best. Two events from the last two weeks have reminded me that Courageous Optimism has no limitations, and these two incidents did not rely on a badge.

The first unfolded in the surf off Seabright Beach in Santa Cruz, California. A 16-year-old lifeguard named Ryder Williams was first into the water when a 10-year-old boy was overtaken by 10-foot shorebreak. Wave after wave buried them both. Bystanders attempted to help and were repelled by the same swells that nearly pulled Williams under, yet his resolve did not waver, and he did not release his grip. A second lifeguard, Aaron Bohnen, fought his way out to the pair, and the three returned to shore together. Williams did not seek a fundraiser, an interview circuit, or a headline. He climbed back into his tower and finished his shift. This is a young man who was not just driven by courageous optimism, but is also humble.

The second unfolded at an In-N-Out in Twin Falls, Idaho, where a gunman opened fire on a lunchtime crowd. Jordan Salinas, a 35-year-old healthcare worker seated nearby with his girlfriend, drew his own weapon when the shooting began. He and an off-duty state trooper returned fire and drove the gunman from the restaurant; law enforcement later credited both men with saving lives before the shooter died by his own hand nearby. Asked afterward whether he'd been afraid, Salinas said he felt no fear at all. “There's a task that needs to be done,” he told a reporter, “and we're the ones who need to do it.”

Neither Williams nor Salinas wears a badge. Neither trained at a police academy. Yet both are, in the fullest sense, empirical demonstrations of the theory built to explain why police officers run toward danger. This suggests the theory is not just a law enforcement phenomenon that requires a badge for an actionable response towards imminent life-threatening circumstances. It is a human capacity that can be drawn upon by anyone with the self-determination, the self-efficacy, and the courage to act despite fear.

What tends to get lost in the celebration of moments like these, however, is the piece of the theory that matters most to anyone hoping to become capable of the same response: None of this arrives from nowhere. Popular narrative treats heroism as a switch that flips in an ordinary person at a dangerous moment to perform an extraordinary act. The evidence says otherwise. Research on self-efficacy holds that our belief in our capacity to execute a given action under pressure is built, incrementally, through prior mastery experience, not summoned whole in a crisis. Williams did not discover rescue techniques mid-wave; he had drilled these actions regularly. Salinas did not discover his resolve at the drive-through window; he built it years earlier, after surviving the 2021 mass shooting at Boise Towne Square mall. That earlier trauma did not leave him fragile, but rather anti-fragile. It left him determined to overhaul his firearms training, rehearse a mental framework for exactly this contingency, and adopt a personal creed he had posted publicly two years before anyone knew his name: “Train like your life depends on it, because God forbid, one day it might. Stay free, stay safe, stay frosty.” Salinas did not just survive adversity; he benefited from and excelled because of it.

Salinas’s ethos is Courageous Optimism compressed into 11 words, and it names what self-determination theory would predict of someone who has internalized both competence and autonomy as governing values. Moral will and moral skill are not dispositions we either have or lack; they are cultivated, in the ordinary hours no one is watching, through practice repetitions, mental rehearsal, and a decision made well in advance about who one intends to be if the worst hour of a stranger's life happens to coincide with one's own. Salinas did not decide against victimhood the moment the shooting began. He decided to be a victor years earlier. The moment simply asked him to keep the promise.

I resist viewing incidents like these as actions by “extraordinary people.” Doing so lets the rest of us off the hook. The more rigorous, and frankly more useful, belief is that self-determination and self-efficacy are trainable constructs, and that ordinary people who invest in them ahead of time become capable of extraordinary acts when the moment arrives uninvited. A teenager on lifeguard duty and a healthcare worker on his lunch break did not draw on some reserve of exceptional courage in reaction to crisis. They responded intentionally by drawing on ordinary courage, disciplined by deliberate preparation, aimed at a moment neither of them chose.

I offer these two recent accounts not for admiration, though Williams and Salinas should both be admired, but as an invitation. Somewhere ahead of you sits a moment that will ask you to be more than a witness to someone else's crisis—smaller, probably, than a mass shooting or a riptide, but no less consequential to the person living through it. Courageous Optimism does not ask whether you will be brave enough when that moment comes. It asks whether you are doing the quiet work now that will make bravery available to you then.

item.title: The Power of Setting Intentions
item.description:
Self-Help

The Power of Setting Intentions

How one daily habit, one simple mindset shift, can change your life.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Our expectations tend to shape our reality.
  • Setting intentions takes advantage of the natural power of positive expectations.
  • Aligning our intentions with our values keeps us focused on our highest selves and living our best life.

I have had a daily writing practice for many years. Like many of you, I'm sure, I filled many a diary as a child and young teen. As a young girl, I documented summer days of tree-climbing and frog-catching, playing hide and seek with the neighbors until the streetlights came on, indicating it was time to go home. As a teen, my writing captured heartbreaks and fashion trends, slights from girlfriends, a teacher's encouragement. To this day, I spend an hour every morning before sunrise writing. Now my pages fill with musings about my children and grandchildren, preparations for upcoming talks, podcasts, and workshops, and trying out topics for essays and opinion pieces.

Setting intentions is not the same as goal-setting

But something else important is happening here. Amidst all the charting and description, I am also setting an intention for the day. I am thinking about what I need to let go: what worries I am carrying that are really not worth the space I've been giving them. In doing so, I am making room for what is important and true and worth my time. I am not naming what needs to be done that day. I am writing about how I want to move through the world that day. I am not writing a "to do" list as much as I am creating a "to be" list.

Setting an intention is setting a tone

An intention is a guidepost, a plan, a reminder you give yourself of who you are and what kind of human being you will present to the world. Your intention may be one of kindness, of care and concern. It may be one of strength and courage. Or it may include creativity, innovation and curiosity. Your day will then proceed along these lines. If your intention involves kindness, your subconscious will look for ways to be helpful: slowing down to hold a door, smiling at the grocery clerk. If it involves strength and courage, you'll notice you are walking straighter, your shoulders set back, your head tall, your confidence following your stance which flowed from your intention. If your intention involved creativity, you will notice details today that escaped you yesterday. You will make connections between disparate objects or scenes or overheard conversations that may help you solve a problem or move a writing project forward.

Aligning our intentions with our values

The most effective intentions emanate from our deeply held beliefs, our core values. In setting an intention, you are projecting a worldview and making a commitment to yourself and those around you that you will live your best life today, be your best self, and bring your best values to your work as you go. As our day gets busy and pressures invariably creep in, our intentions act as a kind of North star, helping to remind us of what is important and true in our world.

When expectations become reality

The expectations we bring with us to a particular situation often shape the reality we perceive in that situation. If we prime ourselves for a certain outcome, we tend to see that version of reality, our senses predetermined to see and hear what we expect. Thus, intention-setting can be thought of as harnessing this very human capacity of positive thinking.

Creating your own daily intention

At the beginning of every yoga class at my gym, our instructor asks us to set an intention for the class. She is asking us to bring a mindset, an attitude to the class that will shape our practice into the most positive experience possible. We are doing something similar here in setting intentions for our day. In choosing a word or phrase that will form this intention, think of your values. Try to answer the question "What do I stand for?" How can I bring my best self to show up for my family and friends? What phrase can I hold in my heart that I can turn to if I'm faced with a challenge or experience a stressor in my day? What can I tell myself that will remind me of my core values, bring out my innate or show my colleagues or co-workers my best self?

Now choose your value, craft your intention, and let this powerful practice bring out the best in you as you share yourself with the world.

item.title: Why People Stop Bringing Their Ideas to Work
item.description:
Creativity

Why People Stop Bringing Their Ideas to Work

Learned silence is debilitating. Here are three things we can do about it.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Silence in meetings often stems from learned responses to past negative experiences, not apathy.
  • Pitching ideas first to a trusted colleague reduces risk and builds confidence for group sharing.
  • Building on others’ ideas is a low-risk way to re-enter conversations and encourage participation.

I remember it like it was yesterday. That big meeting where the client flew in from outside the country to our office to hear a presentation. It was amazing. Catering. Exotic coffee. Presentation slides that were worked on for weeks. The client viewed the material and had a few questions. I knew the answer. So I piped up. It was my moment. The moment that would change everything.

Yet I got flattened.

The agency director stepped all over my answer, minimized it, and moved on. The thing is, I didn't decide to stop contributing. I learned to. One bad experience is enough. Many bad experiences like that? Over time? Yep. People stop contributing. The brain is efficient1, it files "that hurt, don't repeat it," and avoids it like the plague.

The silence you see in your meetings? That silence isn't apathy. It's memory.

So how do we break through and regain the ability for people to be reenergized to bring new ideas to work? How do we break through the learned silence? Here are three ideas to get everyone participating.

1. Start Small

Not every big idea has big origins. Sometimes it's OK to have a small idea blossom into a larger idea later. Starting small enables you to test-drive your idea in a lower-risk environment. So I recommend that people try their ideas with one trusted person first. Start small.

When people have ideas they'd like to contribute, groups are often the worst venue for introducing them, yet meetings are frequently the only venue most people try. Take it to one colleague first, not to get approval, but to find out where it's weak when the cost of being wrong is one person's reaction instead of 13. Then you can bring it back with a second voice already attached.

Be open to the feedback that you may hear. Be curious about what you may learn. You may not get the response you expected, but feel free to evolve the idea with the new feedback. Recent research2 found that people often struggle to accept criticism because our brains naturally see it as a threat. Yet by understanding this bias and approaching feedback with curiosity, we can turn criticism into a powerful tool for learning and growth.

Another great bonus is that the person you tested the idea with may often speak up in the room in support, and an idea with two people behind it lands differently than an idea with one.

2. 10 Bad Ideas

Write down 10 ideas a day. Some of them may be bad ideas, some of them may be good ideas. But that is not the point. After so long, you stop generating ideas because generating ideas hurts when there is no outlet. So instead, create an outlet for your ideas even if no one gets to hear them at first.

Writing down ideas makes them real. A study out of the University of Missouri3 found that the human brain's working memory can actively hold only three to five meaningful pieces of information at once. This limited capacity helps explain why people struggle with ideation and highlights the importance of organizing information into meaningful chunks by writing things down.

Once you have done this for a week or two, look at the inventory of ideas you have come up with. There should be plenty there to pick from.

Now it's time to get right back in the mix and fire off a few ideas. Stepping out and trying ideas is much more comfortable when there are tons of ideas in your inventory. The rebuilt supply is there to help you in case an idea gets shot down—but no worries, another idea is on its way.

What actually atrophies during long silence isn't courage, it's idea production. When we use my 10 bad ideas concept, we create a space and a freedom for ourselves to make ideas a regular part of our production at work without worrying about any one of them being a superstar.

3. Build, Don’t Launch

Take an existing idea and enrich it. When someone else offers an idea, you attach to it and extend it. "Building on what Dana said, if we're moving the timeline, the vendor conversation has to happen this week." It’s a low-stakes way to get back in the game.

If your idea extension gets shot down, they're not rejecting you for going out on a limb. They're adjusting a group idea. That's a survivable outcome, and survivable outcomes are what help rebuild the pattern of idea participation in the first place.

Yet here is the thing with this idea: Agreeable people are pleasant, yet ignored. And it turns out that disagreeable people fare far worse. One study even found that disagreeable people at work do not have any advantages4. So what can you do? Attach to only one idea per meeting, every so often. Use this to bridge the gap between your idea and latching on to someone else’s.

Thinking back to the big launch we had many years ago and getting flattened for contributing an idea, I wish I had known about the three tools listed above.

Contributing ideas to the conversation should never be painful; it should be part and parcel of your everyday work. Yet sometimes the environment for ideation is not ideal. In those cases, the three ideas above will give you a road map for sharing new ideas and give leadership a road map for incubating them among staff.

At the end of the day, ideas are the currency of a business. And energizing ideas, especially in the world of AI, is a must in today’s business landscape.

item.title: What If We’ve Been Talking About Masculinity All Wrong?
item.description:
Gender

What If We’ve Been Talking About Masculinity All Wrong?

Why the need to achieve manhood may be the problem, not the solution.

Posted August 4, 2026

Key points
  • Masculinity is not fixed; different masculinities shape how men think, feel, and behave.
  • The pressure to prove manhood can leave men vulnerable to shame and insecurity.
  • Modern men need models of masculinities that embrace cooperation, purpose, and growth.
  • There is growing recognition that masculinities can be built on care, connection, and creating value.

It’s a fine winter's morning, crisp and bright. It's the type of day that requires both gloves and sunglasses. I’ve just walked out of Belfast’s Grand Central train station. Through the mist of my evaporating breath, I can see seven labourers in high-vis jackets and hard hats completing the walkway outside the new station. Some are pushing wheelbarrows of stones; others use mallets to position paving slabs. Nearby, four taxi drivers stand beside their cars. One takes a drag on a cigarette while another discusses yesterday’s football results. There’s banter and cajoling.

I continue up the street. A couple walk arm-in-arm towards me, wearing the same brand of jacket in different colours—black and pink. I smile and say hello. Passing a clothes alteration shop, I glance through the window. Six sewing machines are laid out, though only two are in use. Between their rhythmic clicks, I hear a Tina Turner song playing in the background.

It’s just another Tuesday morning in Belfast.

Quick question: How many men and women did I remember from that morning?

Take a moment to count them.

That’s right—I never mentioned anyone’s gender. But your mind probably inferred it. We all carry expectations about how men, women, and other genders behave, the jobs they do, the things they talk about, and, yes, even the colours of the jackets they wear. From a young age, we are socialised into ideas about masculinity and femininity that shape these expectations.

There’s been a lot of talk about masculinity. Too much, perhaps. The problem is that we keep talking about masculinity when we should be talking about masculinities.

The World Health Organization (2018) defines masculinities as culturally specific sets of attributes, values, and behaviours associated with being a man that influence health, help-seeking, and well-being. Considering the worrying state of boys’ and men’s well-being, masculinities matter. Masculinities also affect the experiences of girls and women. Understanding masculinities helps explain why men behave as they do, sometimes in ways that benefit themselves and others, and sometimes in ways that cause harm.

The word masculine comes from the Latin masculus, meaning "worthy of a man." It’s no surprise, then, that masculinities have often revolved around proving one’s worth.

Anthropologist David D. Gilmore argued that across cultures, manhood is based on what he called a “manhood of achievement” (Gilmore, 1990). Whether it is enduring bullet ant stings among the Sateré-Mawé of the Amazon, hunting a first antelope among the !Kung of the Kalahari Desert, or land diving on Pentecost Island of Vanuatu, becoming a man has often required passing a test. Masculinities are, in many respects, meritocracies.

Across time and culture, men have been stalked by a fear of falling short. Masculinities do more than describe what it means to be a man; they create pressure to continually prove it. Take, for example, Rudyard Kipling’s famous poem "If." It lists more than 20 standards of character before concluding: “you’ll be a Man, my son!” No pressure there.

None of this denies that femininities have also imposed unfair expectations on women. If men have tended to be criticised for failing to meet the mark, women have been criticised for overstepping it: being too ambitious, too assertive, too loud, or too sexual. Nonetheless, achievement-based masculinities can be brittle. During periods of economic or social instability, identities built on success become vulnerable. Ironically, because men have historically occupied positions of power, this vulnerability is sometimes overlooked, even when it is real.

Psychologist Joseph Vandello and colleagues captured this idea in the Precarious Manhood Hypothesis. They argued that, as formal rites of passage to manhood have faded in Western societies, men increasingly seek other ways to demonstrate manhood, including excelling in sport, accumulating wealth, building muscular physiques, sexual conquest, risk-taking, or excessive drinking. Their research studies, conducted with male and female American college students, suggested that manhood is seen as something that must continually be earned and is more easily threatened than womanhood (Vandello et al., 2008). Furthermore, male participants who felt their manhood had been undermined were more likely to respond with aggressive thoughts compared to female participants who had their womanhood questioned.

Rethinking masculinity begins with reflecting on the assumptions we inherit.
Source: Atahan Demir / Pexels

Being a man in a changing world

Famously, David D. Gilmore's ethnographic work across cultures gave rise to the idea that masculinities have historically revolved around three core responsibilities: to procreate, provide, and protect. These “three P's” reinforce the idea that manhood must be achieved. Woe betide the man who cannot have children, loses his job, or cannot protect those around him. But the world has changed since Gilmore conducted his fieldwork. Recent decades have brought important progress for girls and women. Alongside these gains—but not because of them—many boys and men have experienced growing uncertainty about their role, status, and purpose. As the feminist author Susan Faludi observed, many men have lost “a useful role in public life, a way of earning a decent and reliable living, appreciation in the home, [and] respectful treatment in the culture” (Faludi, 2011).

The issue is not that women have advanced; it is that some men perceive, and sometimes experience, a loss of direction. But metaphorically speaking, a pencil should not fear the development of the pen; it should fear losing its own sharpness. Rather than tying our identity to a shrinking set of roles or achievements, we men can remain sharp by cultivating adaptability, competence, contribution, and purpose.

Not everyone responds to change in the same way. Some men adapt. Others resist. Still others appeal to a return to the "good old days." This longing has been described as radical nostalgia—the belief that reviving past cultural norms will solve present problems. But, as investigative journalist Jim Hougan warned, radical nostalgia often “falsifies the past” (Hougan, 1975) and becomes an escape from action rather than a guide for it. Going back is no way to move forward. Our task is not to recreate our grandfathers, but to cultivate the strengths boys and men need today.

Increasingly, social scientists suggest that masculinities should be understood less as fixed roles and more as the ability to adapt behaviour to changing contexts. When viewed this way, Gilmore’s "three P's" become guiding principles rather than rigid expectations, and a fourth P naturally emerges: prosocial.

Beyond the 'three P's': Recognising masculinity as a prosocial force

The drive to procreate can be understood more broadly as creating value: parenting, mentoring, coaching, teaching, innovating, making art, or caring for the environment. Protecting means promoting the safety, dignity, and rights of others—challenging abuse, supporting vulnerable people, and fostering psychologically safe workplaces. Providing extends beyond earning money to giving time, care, emotional presence, and practical support to partners, families, and communities.

Seen in this light, modern masculinities are fundamentally about cooperation, Homo co-operans if you like. We are called to:

  • Co-create a shared future rather than merely consume the present.
  • Champion the safety and dignity of others by using our strengths, physical, intellectual, social, and moral.
  • Contribute meaningfully to the people, families, and communities we belong to.

This vision aligns with the growing idea of caring masculinities (Doucet, 2006), which emphasise caregiving, emotional openness, and a rejection of dominance and violence. Some fear this represents an attempt to emasculate men. They would do well to heed the advice, “Be completely humble and gentle; be patient, bearing with one another in love.” These words weren’t penned by a new-age guru; they were written in the first century A.D. by Saint Paul.

This is not about men becoming soft. It is about recognising that strength without compassion is brittle, and that the best masculinities are those that enable men, and everyone around them, to thrive.
